Health_Implications_and_Significance: No direct health effect, but elevated temperatures promote bacterial regrowth, enhance pipe corrosion, and intensify taste and odor complaints.
Major_Sources: Ambient atmospheric conditions, solar radiation, industrial thermal discharge.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: No health-based guideline value set. Cool water is generally more palatable and limits microbial proliferation.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: No direct health impact within normal ranges. Acidic water (pH < 6.5) causes heavy metal pipe corrosion (lead/copper leaching); alkaline water (pH > 8.5) causes bitter taste, scaling, and decreases chlorine disinfection efficiency.
Major_Sources: Natural mineral geology (carbonate/bicarbonate balance), acidic deposition, industrial effluent.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Operational guideline. Optimum pH 6.5–8.5 ensures stable distribution networks and effective primary disinfection.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: High turbidity shields pathogenic viruses, bacteria, and protozoan cysts from chemical disinfection (chlorine/UV) and stimulates microbial regrowth.
Major_Sources: Silt, clay, suspended particulate matter, soil erosion, runoff.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Aesthetic threshold is 5 NTU. For terminal disinfection, median turbidity should ideally be < 0.2–1 NTU to ensure 99.9% pathogen kill.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Direct indicator of total dissolved ionic species. High conductivity is associated with excessive salinity, scaling, and corrosive potential.
Major_Sources: Mineral dissolution from bedrock, saline intrusion, agricultural runoff.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Directly proportional to TDS (TDS ≈ 0.55–0.7 × EC). Acceptability upper threshold is typically around 1500 µS/cm.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Not of direct health concern at normal drinking levels. Levels above 1000 mg/L impart an unpalatable mineral taste and cause household pipe encrustation.
Major_Sources: Dissolved inorganic salts (calcium, magnesium, potassium, sodium, bicarbonates, chlorides, sulfates).
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: <300 mg/L: excellent; 300–600 mg/L: good; 600–900 mg/L: fair; 900–1200 mg/L: poor; >1200 mg/L: unacceptable.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Hardness primarily mitigates cardiovascular risks; high hardness (>500 mg/L) causes excessive scaling in plumbing, water heaters, and requires more soap.
Major_Sources: Dissolution of limestone (calcite) and dolomite formations.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Soft water (<60 mg/L) may be corrosive; water >500 mg/L is generally rejected by consumers due to mineral taste and scale.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Essential mineral for bone development and cardiac rhythm. High levels contribute to water hardness and scale deposition.
Major_Sources: Sedimentary rocks, limestone, gypsum, calcite.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: WHO does not propose a health-based guideline value because drinking water is a minor source compared to dietary intake.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Essential cofactor in human metabolic enzymes. High magnesium combined with sulfate exerts a transient laxative effect.
Major_Sources: Dolomite, magnesite, igneous and sedimentary minerals.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: No health-based guideline value is set by WHO. High levels give water an astringent or bitter taste.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Essential electrolyte. Concentrations > 200 mg/L may pose health considerations for individuals on strict sodium-restricted diets (hypertension/heart failure).
Major_Sources: Halite deposits, sea salt intrusion, water softening chemicals (ion exchange).
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Taste threshold is 200 mg/L. No health-based guideline value is derived as diet represents the dominant route of intake.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Crucial intracellular cation. Drinking water levels are rarely a risk except for susceptible individuals with kidney failure or hyperkalemia.
Major_Sources: Silicate minerals, potash fertilizers, agricultural runoff.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Concentrations in drinking-water are generally well below those of health concern.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: High concentrations impart a salty taste and increase electrical conductivity, accelerating corrosion of metal pipes and plumbing fittings.
Major_Sources: Halite rock dissolution, marine saltwater intrusion, road deicing salts, sewage discharge.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: No health-based guideline value proposed; 250 mg/L is established based on taste detection.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Levels above 500 mg/L can induce dehydration and osmotic diarrhea in unacclimated consumers, particularly infants.
Major_Sources: Gypsum, anhydrite, industrial mining discharge, atmospheric sulfur deposition.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Taste impairment occurs at 250 mg/L for sodium/potassium sulfate. WHO advises authorities to be notified if levels exceed 500 mg/L.

WHO_Guideline_Value: 50 mg/L as NO₃⁻ (or 11 mg/L as Nitrate-N)
Health_Implications_and_Significance: Causes methemoglobinemia ('blue-baby syndrome') in bottle-fed infants by oxidizing hemoglobin into methemoglobin; suspected precursor to carcinogenic nitrosamines.
Major_Sources: Agricultural fertilizers, animal feedlots, septic tank leakage, municipal sewage.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Health-based limit. If nitrite is also present, the combined ratio [NO3]/50 + [NO2]/3 must not exceed 1.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Concentrations above 1.5 mg/L produce dental fluorosis (enamel mottling); long-term intake > 4–10 mg/L leads to severe, debilitating skeletal fluorosis.
Major_Sources: Geological weathering of fluorite, apatite, volcanic rocks; industrial emissions.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Health-based guideline value. In hot climates with high water consumption, national limits are often set lower (0.7–1.0 mg/L).

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Essential dietary element with low oral toxicity. Water > 0.3 mg/L stains sanitary ware/laundry, develops reddish-brown turbidity, promotes iron bacteria biofilm growth.
Major_Sources: Natural mineral strata, pyrites, cast iron / ductile iron water distribution pipe corrosion.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: No health-based guideline value derived; 0.3 mg/L is based on severe aesthetic staining and unpleasant metallic taste.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Class 1 human carcinogen. Causes hyperkeratosis, hyperpigmentation, skin/lung/bladder cancers, peripheral neuropathy, and vascular diseases (Blackfoot disease).
Major_Sources: Natural reductive dissolution of arsenic-rich sedimentary aquifer rocks, pesticide residues, mining wastes.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Provisional guideline value due to analytical measurement limitations and treatment achievability in low-resource settings.

WHO_Guideline_Value: Must not be detectable in any 100 mL sample (0)
Health_Implications_and_Significance: Not inherently pathogenic, but serves as a primary sanitary benchmark indicating water treatment breakdown, pipe integrity failure, or biofilm development.
Major_Sources: Feces of warm-blooded animals, organically rich soils, decomposing plant material, biofilms.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Should be non-detectable in 95% of distribution samples collected throughout any 12-month monitoring cycle.

WHO_Guideline_Value: Must not be detectable in any 100 mL sample (0)
Health_Implications_and_Significance: Definitive indicator of recent fecal contamination. Exposure risks include severe gastroenteritis, bloody diarrhea, cholera, and hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS).
Major_Sources: Human feces, livestock manure, sewage overflow, unlined latrines near water table.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Zero tolerance parameter. Detection triggers immediate boil-water orders, system chlorine re-dosing, and sanitary surveys.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Neurotoxic cumulative poison. Produces irreversible neurodevelopmental damage and IQ loss in children; causes hypertension, cardiovascular mortality, and nephropathy in adults.
Major_Sources: Corrosion of lead service lines, lead-bearing brass fixtures, and lead-soldered plumbing joints.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Health-based limit. Because lead has no known biological threshold of safety, concentrations should be kept as low as reasonably practicable.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Target organ is the kidney (renal tubular damage). Inorganic mercury also induces central nervous system toxicity, tremors, and cognitive dysfunction.
Major_Sources: Artisanal gold mining, coal combustion emissions, dental amalgams, industrial effluents.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Applies specifically to total inorganic mercury. Organic forms (methylmercury) are primarily ingested via seafood rather than drinking water.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Accumulates in the renal cortex, causing irreversible kidney tubular dysfunction, proteinuria, osteomalacia, bone brittleness ('Itai-itai' disease).
Major_Sources: Galvanized pipe corrosion, nickel-cadmium batteries, phosphate fertilizer contamination, industrial electroplating.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Health-based guideline value based on human epidemiological studies evaluating lifetime renal accumulation.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Hexavalent chromium [Cr(VI)] is a potent carcinogen via inhalation and classified as probably carcinogenic via ingestion; causes severe allergic contact dermatitis and liver/kidney toxicity.
Major_Sources: Tanneries, industrial metal finishing, stainless steel production, chrome pigments.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Provisional guideline value for total chromium. Retained under review in recent GDWQ addenda as toxicological data on Cr(VI) ingestion evolve.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Causes systemic contact dermatitis in nickel-sensitized individuals (flare-ups of eczema); potential nephrotoxic and reproductive effects at elevated doses.
Major_Sources: Leaching from nickel-plated household taps, plumbing fittings, stainless steel, geological minerals.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Revised and confirmed in the 4th edition 2nd addendum. Protective against both acute allergic reactions in sensitive individuals and chronic kidney effects.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Short-term ingestion causes acute gastrointestinal irritation, nausea, and vomiting; chronic high doses lead to hepatic and renal damage, especially in patients with Wilson's disease.
Major_Sources: Internal corrosion of residential copper piping, brass fixtures, industrial wastewater.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Health-based limit is 2.0 mg/L. Blue/green staining of fixtures and astringent taste typically occur at 1.0–2.0 mg/L.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Essential trace nutrient with low mammalian toxicity. Concentrations above 3 mg/L impart a sharp metallic astringent taste and cause milky opalescence.
Major_Sources: Dezincification of brass plumbing, galvanized iron pipe leaching, industrial plating.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: No health-based guideline value set. Water containing zinc above 3–5 mg/L may develop an iridescent greasy film on boiling.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Neurotoxin that impairs neurological development, motor function, and cognitive performance in young children. Also causes black staining and deposits.
Major_Sources: Naturally occurring mineral deposits, reductive dissolution in deep anaerobic wells, industrial discharge.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Updated in 2021/2022 WHO background review from historical 0.4 mg/L down to 0.08 mg/L to protect infant neurodevelopment. Staining occurs at > 0.05 mg/L.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Health-based value (0.9 mg/L) is well above practical treatment achievable targets. Residual alum precipitates cause milky discoloration and floc deposition in mains.
Major_Sources: Aluminum-based coagulants (alum / polyaluminum chloride) used in municipal water clarification; natural bauxite minerals.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Operational target to avoid post-filtration precipitation. Dialysis patients require strict exclusion (<0.01 mg/L) to prevent dialysis encephalopathy.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Essential trace nutrient, but chronic excess causes selenosis, characterized by brittle hair, dystrophic nails, garlic odor of breath, and peripheral neurological symptoms.
Major_Sources: Cretaceous shale weathering, agricultural drainage from seleniferous soils, mining wastes.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Provisional guideline value revised to 0.04 mg/L in 4th edition addenda.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Causes abdominal cramps, vomiting, diarrhea, altered blood glucose/cholesterol, and cardiac arrhythmia following acute/sub-chronic exposure.
Major_Sources: Leaching from antimony-tin solders in pipes, PET plastic bottle manufacturing catalysts, industrial flame retardants.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Health-based guideline value based on subchronic oral rodent toxicity studies.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Induces vasoconstriction, leading to hypertension and adverse cardiac muscle effects; chronic toxicological target is renal nephropathy.
Major_Sources: Natural barite geological formations, oil/gas drilling mud lubricants, industrial discharge.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: Guideline value revised to 1.3 mg/L in the 4th edition (incorporating addenda) based on benchmark dose calculation for nephropathy.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: No acute systemic toxicity, but excessive chronic ingestion results in argyria—an irreversible blue-grey discoloration of the skin and mucous membranes.
Major_Sources: Silver-impregnated point-of-use ceramic filters, electronic effluent, photography wastes.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: No health-based guideline value established. WHO notes that lifetime exposure below 0.1 mg/L does not cause argyria.

Health_Implications_and_Significance: Essential component of vitamin B12 (cobalamin). High doses can cause polycythemia, goiter, and cardiomyopathy; however, concentrations in drinking water are extremely low.
Major_Sources: Lithium-ion battery recycling, metal alloys, mining tailings, coal burning.
WHO_Remarks_and_Notes: WHO has not established a drinking water guideline because cobalt levels in public water supplies are well below concentrations of toxicological concern.
